name: Threat Model Reviewer v2.1.3
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer 2.1.3

Appearance and reach. The app can now be themed, a question can be asked without leaving the
tab you are on, and comparing two revisions is legible.

The deterministic guarantee is unchanged: the verdict and the 0–100 score come from the rubric
engine alone. Nothing in this release touches how a model is scored.

Highlights

Light, Dark and Match Windows

Help → Appearance. The choice is remembered between sessions, applies immediately without a
restart, and Match Windows follows the operating system as it changes.

This took three attempts, and the reasons are worth recording because they are not obvious:

  • WPF freezes brushes declared in a XAML resource dictionary wherever it can, and a frozen brush
    cannot be recoloured. Mutating the palette in place did nothing at all.
  • StaticResource resolves exactly once, at load. Swapping the dictionary afterwards left the
    already-built window — and every control style — on the colours it started with. This is why an
    early build changed the page background and kept white buttons with white labels on them.

The palette is therefore owned at runtime and referenced with DynamicResource, which is what
lets a switch reach the whole window instantly.

A floating Ask panel

A launcher in the bottom-left opens a compact chat over any tab, so asking a question no longer
costs you your place in the Findings list or the Fix queue.

It is deliberately not a second assistant. The panel and the Ask tab share one view model, so
there is one conversation: maximise hands the history to the tab rather than starting again,
and anything asked in the tab is already there when the panel is reopened. As in the tab, common
questions are answered straight from the model's own numbers with no AI call, and are labelled as
such.

Compare, made legible

  • "Use open model" now applies to both fields. Comparing the open model against an older
    revision is as common as the reverse, and only the baseline supported it.
  • A swap button, for when the two revisions go in the wrong way round.
  • The results now lead with the verdict and separate what got worse from what got better,
    rather than stacking dense lists of long strings under a table.

Fixed

Issue Detail
Duplicated interaction labels An interaction with no name falls back to source → target for its name, and the row then printed that same string again underneath. Named flows were unaffected, which is why it read as intentional.
Ragged Overview statistics Eight fixed-width tiles in a wrap panel broke 5 + 3, leaving a visible hole. They now sit on an even four-column grid.
Ask panel outlived its model Closing a model left the floating panel open over the empty state with nothing to answer about.

Under the hood

Theming forced a cleanup that was overdue. Every colour in the app now resolves through a
semantic token rather than being written where it is used:

  • 114 hard-coded colours in the main window
  • 26 white backgrounds across the dialogs
  • 43 literals chosen in view models for grades, severity and progress bars

That last group is the subtle one. Those values were bound through a hex-to-brush converter,
which produced a brush no theme owned — so they alone kept their light-mode colour after a
switch, one layer deeper than the markup fix reached.

The diagram is exempt by design. It renders a document rather than application chrome, and
its element colours are not ours to re-theme. The guard names the exemption explicitly instead of
leaving it to chance.

New regression guards cover each way this fails quietly: the two palettes must define the same
tokens and must differ on the core surfaces (so a copied palette cannot pass as "dark"), no
themed brush may be bound with StaticResource, no colour may be hard-coded in the main window
or the view models, and the floating panel must share the tab's conversation.

1249 tests, no warnings.

Install

Download below. The MSI is recommended for most users; the portable zip needs no installer.

Existing installations will be offered this update in-app.

The binaries are signed with a self-signed certificate, so SmartScreen shows a warning on first
run. This is disclosed rather than worked around — a self-signed certificate never accrues
reputation. A publicly trusted certificate is on the roadmap.

Verifying what it sends

Unchanged from 2.1.0: no telemetry, no analytics. The only outbound requests are the GitHub
release check, your own Copilot seat, and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint if you configure one.
See DATA-HANDLING.md.

name: Threat Model Reviewer v2.1.2
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer v2.1.2

Release date: 23 August 2026 · Platform: Windows 10/11 x64 · Type: Patch — fixes found by
driving the app before shipping, rather than trusting a green test suite.

Threat Model Reviewer reviews, fixes and analyzes Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool (.tm7) threat
models — and OWASP Threat Dragon (.json) — catching the issues a Microsoft SDL reviewer would
send back before you submit. The readiness verdict and 0–100 score are deterministic and
computed entirely on your machine.

At a glance

Item Detail
Why update History recorded nothing, and the assistant showed raw Markdown
Who should update Everyone on 2.1.x
Score impact None. No scoring behaviour changed
Rollback Install any earlier 2.x package; configuration is forward/backward compatible

Fixed

History recorded nothing

Two separate faults, and the first is the more instructive one.

The store, the query layer, the privacy controls and the History tab were all complete and all
tested — and nothing ever called the recorder. Every unit test passed, the build was clean, and
the feature did nothing. The gap was between the code existing and the code running.

Then, once recording worked, the tab still appeared empty because it only loaded when you pressed
Refresh. Reviewing a model now records it, and opening the tab loads it.

The assistant showed its own Markdown

Answers are written in Markdown and were bound straight to text, so you saw **NOT READY** and
literal dashes instead of formatted text — which made the most important line in an answer the
hardest to read. The app already had a Markdown renderer used elsewhere; the Ask tab now uses it.

The test suite wrote into your real history

Wiring the recorder into model loading meant any test that opened a model recorded a review into
%LOCALAPPDATA%, so running the suite filled a developer's History tab with fixture models.

The history root now honours THREATMODELREVIEWER_HISTORY_ROOT. The tests redirect it to a
temp folder, and administrators can use the same variable to move history off a roaming profile.

Compare's buttons looked broken

Explain with Copilot and Export are correctly disabled until a comparison exists, but
nothing said so. They now explain themselves while disabled, and the Baseline and Candidate boxes
accept a dropped .tm7 — picking two revisions through a dialog twice is tedious when both files
are already in the same folder.

A documented claim was untrue

The docs said generate produces a NOT READY model "by construction". It does not. A generated
model reports READY WITH NOTES with zero gating findings, because the rubric counts Needs
Investigation as triaged — it is a deliberate disposition, not an absence of one.

That is worth understanding rather than glossing over: a generated model is structurally
complete, which is what the readiness gate measures. It is not a reviewed model. Nobody has
looked at those threats yet. Treat generation as a starting point for triage.

The coverage matrix was labelled with the wrong edition

It read "OWASP Top 10 (2021)" while listing the 2025 categories introduced in 2.1.1.

Added

Feature wiring tests

The History bug could not have been caught by unit tests — every part passed in isolation. So this
release adds a different kind of test, asserting that each capability is reachable from a surface
a user can actually drive:

  • every Core engine referenced by the app or the CLI,
  • every advertised tab present and not collapsed,
  • every CLI verb dispatchable,
  • the history recorder actually invoked when a model is reviewed,
  • the assistant rendering Markdown rather than printing it,
  • the History tab index matching its real position in the tab strip.

They cannot prove a feature is correct — only that it is not orphaned. That is precisely the class
of failure that produced an empty History tab in a fully tested build.

Verify your download

Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\ThreatModelReviewer-v2.1.2-x64.msi | Format-List Status, SignerCertificate
Get-FileHash .\ThreatModelReviewer-v2.1.2-x64.msi -Algorithm SHA256

Upgrading

Install over the top; settings, credentials and preferences are preserved. No model file format
changes, so existing .tm7 files and saved reports are unaffected.

name: Threat Model Reviewer v2.1.1
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer v2.1.1

Release date: 23 August 2026 · Platform: Windows 10/11 x64 · Type: Patch — fixes three
issues that prevented users from reaching what 2.1.0 shipped, and corrects the standards the rubric
cites.

Threat Model Reviewer reviews, fixes and analyzes Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool (.tm7) threat
models — and OWASP Threat Dragon (.json) — catching the issues a Microsoft SDL reviewer would
send back before you submit. The readiness verdict and 0–100 score are deterministic and
computed entirely on your machine.

At a glance

Item Detail
Why update 2.1.0 could fail to install in-app, and its header could hide the tab strip
New in the app Create, Assistant, Compare, Ask and History are now all available
Standards Rubric now cites OWASP Top 10:2025, not the superseded 2021 edition
Score impact None. Both sample models score exactly as before
Rollback Install any earlier 2.x package; configuration is forward/backward compatible

Everything is now in both the app and the CLI

2.1.0 shipped seven engines but only wired them to the command line. They are now in the desktop app
too, so you can choose the surface rather than the feature.

Capability App CLI
Review a threat model Overview / Findings / Fix (default verb)
Create a model Create tab generate
Extract a DFD from a doc, image or OpenAPI spec Assistant tab ingest
Compare two revisions Compare tab compare
Ask questions about a model Ask tab ask
Local review history and trends History tab history
Organisation policy (CLI today) policy
SDL artifact bundle Export menu sdl

Compare

Pick two revisions — or use the model you already have open as the baseline — and see what changed,
what got worse, and what got better, alongside the score and verdict movement. Elements, flows,
boundaries and threats are matched by identity, so a rename reads as a rename rather than a delete
plus an add.

Explain with Copilot adds a plain-English read of the change. The numbers are computed before
Copilot is asked and are never altered by it; the narrative is labelled as advisory. Exports to
HTML, Markdown or CSV.

Ask

An assistant scoped to the threat model you have open. Common questions — your score, why a model is
not ready, how many threats are unmitigated, which flows cross a trust boundary — are answered
straight from the model's own numbers with no AI call at all, so no answer can contradict the
review. Every reply says which of the two it was.

Open-ended questions go to Copilot, grounded in the same facts and required to cite them.

History

Every review you run, recorded locally, with a per-model score trend so you can see whether a threat
model is actually improving. The tab states where the data lives and can open that folder — "it never
leaves your machine" is a claim you should be able to verify rather than take on trust. One click
clears it.

Fixed

Updating in-app could produce an unusable installer

If you updated from inside the app and saw

This installation package could not be opened. Verify that the package exists and that you can
access it…

this is the fix. The published 2.1.0 MSI was never faulty — it is byte-identical to the local
build and installs cleanly. The download path was at fault.

The updater only verified a download's size when a length was known. On the release-atom fallback —
taken whenever the anonymous GitHub API hits its limit of 60 requests an hour — every asset size is
reported as 0. If the server also omitted Content-Length, nothing was checked at all, so a
truncated transfer or an error page was written under the asset's name and handed to msiexec.

Downloads are now format-checked before they run: an MSI must begin with the OLE compound-file
signature, a zip with PK, an executable with MZ. When the check fails you get a message naming
the real cause and pointing at the browser download, instead of a dead-end installer error.

The header could collapse and hide the tabs

The identity block sat in a stretchy column beside a content-sized button cluster. Adding the Close
button in 2.1.0 tipped the balance: the cluster claimed the whole row, the stretchy column collapsed
to a few pixels, and "Threat Model Reviewer" wrapped one character per line down the left edge —
pushing the tab strip off screen entirely.

Rebuilt as a single compact strip of roughly 50px in which nothing can wrap. The open model's name
trims with an ellipsis and keeps its full text in a tooltip.

The verdict was printed twice

The CI band is FAIL precisely when the verdict is NOT READY — they are one outcome, not two. Shown
as separate chips they read as two independent failures, and a high-scoring model could show a green
grade pill beside a red FAIL. They are now a single chip.

Markdown was rejected as "not a diagram"

.md is registered as a diagram extension because markdown can embed Mermaid, so plain prose never
reached the document reader. Shared extensions now fall back correctly — and markdown that does
contain a diagram is still read as one.

Changed

Create and Assistant are now available

Both tabs were fully implemented but hidden. With 2.1.0 shipping a round-trip-verified .tm7
writer, there is no longer a reason to keep model authoring out of the product.

  • Create — name your system, start from a template, add components, data flows and trust
    boundaries, refine the whole thing in plain English with Copilot, and watch a live diagram build as
    you go. Generating produces a reviewable .tm7 and opens it immediately.
  • Assistant — extract a data-flow diagram from a document, an architecture image (with a
    vision-capable model), or an OpenAPI spec. Nothing is written without your confirmation.

One generation engine, not two

The Create tab used the original generator while the CLI's generate used the deterministic
pipeline. Two implementations of the same feature drift apart, and anyone comparing them would
rightly lose confidence in both. Create now runs the same pipeline, reports how many threats it
produced, and states plainly that each is recorded as Needs Investigation — an enumerated starting
point for triage, not a finished review.

Rubric cites OWASP Top 10:2025

OWASP published the 2025 edition on 6 November 2025. All 43 references were updated.

The edition re-ranked categories rather than merely renaming them, so they were mapped by
concept — bumping the year in place would have silently mislabelled half of them:

Concept 2021 2025
Broken Access Control A01 A01
Security Misconfiguration A05 A02
Software Supply Chain Failures (was Vulnerable & Outdated Components) A06 A03
Cryptographic Failures A02 A04
Injection A03 A05
Insecure Design A04 A06
Authentication Failures (renamed) A07 A07
Software or Data Integrity Failures A08 A08
Security Logging and Alerting Failures A09 A09
Server-Side Request Forgery A10 folded into A01
Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions — A10 (new)

No scores change. The coverage matrix feeds reports and the assistant's fact sheet, never the
scoring engine, and both sample models score exactly as they did before. Automated guards now assert
the categories against the published list, so this cannot silently rot again.

Release pipeline

Builds now upload their artifacts before publishing, so a missing or expired publishing token costs
a manual publish rather than a repeated multi-minute build.

Verify your download

Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\ThreatModelReviewer-v2.1.1-x64.msi | Format-List Status, SignerCertificate
Get-FileHash .\ThreatModelReviewer-v2.1.1-x64.msi -Algorithm SHA256

Upgrading

Install over the top; settings, credentials and preferences are preserved. No model file format
changes, so existing .tm7 files and saved reports are unaffected.

If you are on 2.1.0 and in-app update failed, download the installer from this page directly — that
path was never affected.

name: Threat Model Reviewer v2.1.0
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer v2.1.0

Release date: 23 August 2026 · Platform: Windows 10/11 x64 · Type: Minor — substantial
new capability, available today through the command line.

Threat Model Reviewer reviews, fixes and analyzes Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool (.tm7) threat
models — and OWASP Threat Dragon (.json) — catching the issues a Microsoft SDL reviewer would
send back before you submit. The readiness verdict and 0–100 score are deterministic and
computed entirely on your machine.

At a glance

Item Detail
What changed Seven new engines: compare, generate, ingest, SDL bundle, ask, history, org policy
Where to use them ThreatModelReviewer.Cli today; the desktop UI for these lands next
Who should update Everyone — this is the current supported release
Risk of updating Low: no change to how existing models are scored or judged
Downtime / migration None. Settings, credentials and preferences are preserved
Rollback Install any earlier 2.0.x package; configuration is forward/backward compatible

Why this release is mostly command line

The engines below are finished and tested, and the desktop surfaces for them are being built next.
Rather than hold working capability back, they ship through the CLI — which is also where they do
the most immediate good, because this is exactly the work a pipeline should be doing on every pull
request.

What's new

Compare two revisions of a threat model

ThreatModelReviewer.Cli compare baseline.tm7 candidate.tm7 --md report.md

Answers the question a reviewer actually has when version 2 arrives: what changed, and did the
security posture get better or worse? Elements, flows, boundaries and threats are matched by
stable identity rather than list position, so a rename is reported as a rename instead of a delete
plus an add.

It reports rubric deltas including pass→fail transitions, threat state changes, and a posture
summary. Exit code 2 on a serious regression, so CI can block on it.

Generate a threat model from a described system

ThreatModelReviewer.Cli generate system.json --out model.tm7

Deterministic STRIDE enumeration keyed on element kinds, trust boundary crossings and flow
properties. Generating twice from the same spec produces byte-identical output.

Every generated threat is recorded as Needs Investigation, and the summary says so plainly: this
is an enumerated starting point, not a completed review. An owner still has to confirm each threat,
decide on a mitigation or a justified exclusion, and record the evidence.

Ingest what your team already has

ThreatModelReviewer.Cli ingest architecture.drawio
ThreatModelReviewer.Cli ingest main.bicep
ThreatModelReviewer.Cli ingest design-doc.docx --out grounding.md
  • Documents — Word, PowerPoint, Excel, PDF, CSV, Markdown, JSON, YAML.
  • Diagrams — Excalidraw, draw.io (including its compressed form), Mermaid, Visio, Graphviz.
    Mapped to data-flow-diagram candidates; anything that cannot be classified confidently is flagged
    for a human rather than guessed at.
  • Infrastructure as code — ARM, Bicep, Terraform. Extracts deterministic security facts with
    a file and line citation for each: TLS enforcement, public network access, identity type,
    key-vault protection, firewall rules. Exit code 2 when insecure configuration is found.

All of it is hardened against hostile input: archive entry, size and ratio caps, DTD processing
prohibited, and no external reference resolution.

Produce the artifacts a reviewer asks for

ThreatModelReviewer.Cli sdl model.tm7 --out ./sdl-bundle

A full threat model document (Markdown and HTML), the threat register (CSV and JSON), an assumptions
and out-of-scope log, a traceability matrix, and a manifest recording the tool version, rubric
version, and the source model's identity and SHA-256 — so a reviewer can verify every file and
reproduce the deterministic content.

Ask questions, answered without AI

ThreatModelReviewer.Cli ask model.tm7 "why is it not ready?"

Common questions are answered exactly from a computed fact sheet, with the supporting check ids
cited — no model call, no network, and no possibility of a hallucinated number contradicting the
engine. Questions that genuinely need judgement are declined rather than guessed at.

Organisation policy, with disclosure that cannot be switched off

ThreatModelReviewer.Cli policy validate my-org.policy.json
ThreatModelReviewer.Cli policy apply model.tm7 --policy my-org.policy.json

Organisations can tune the rubric to their own risk appetite. Waivers require a reason, an
owner and an expiry — an expired waiver stops applying and becomes a finding of its own.

Applying a policy always prints the unpoliced result beside the policed one, together with every
suppression and the policy's hash. A policy can adjust the rubric, but it can never quietly hide a
failure. Ships default, strict, and a worked enterprise-exceptions preset.

Local review history

ThreatModelReviewer.Cli history --trend <model>

Append-only, on your machine only, never transmitted. File paths are hashed rather than stored
by default, and AI prompts and responses are never recorded.

Also in this release

  • Close the open threat model (Ctrl+W), with an unsaved-changes guard. Previously a model could
    only be replaced, never closed.
  • Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool stencil artwork in the diagram view, extracted at run time from
    your own MTMT installation. The artwork is Microsoft's and is never redistributed with this app.
  • File attachments in the Edit with Copilot panel, so you can hand over the diagram or document
    you already have instead of describing it.
  • Model Context Protocol support, shipped disabled. Each server must be enabled individually and
    states plainly what it can see.
  • GitHub Copilot SDK 1.0.11, moving the bundled runtime to Copilot CLI 1.0.79.
  • Fluent 2 design foundation across the app.

Fixed

  • A WCAG contrast failure that was shipping. The score and band chips used colours failing AA
    against their own background (2.78:1 and 4.29:1). All three states now pass (5.64:1, 4.55:1,
    6.40:1).
  • An unreadable model dropdown, which showed raw record text inside a 190px control.
  • A gap in the archive guard: a crafted Office file whose directory under-reported an entry's
    size passed inspection and then silently truncated content. That mismatch is now rejected.
  • Markdown ingestion, which was rejected as "not a diagram" because .md can embed Mermaid.
  • Documentation on the score, verdict and CI band: the FAIL band and the NOT READY verdict
    are the same outcome, not two independent ones.

Exit codes

Uniform across every command, so pipelines can act on them:

Code Meaning
0 Succeeded, nothing gating
1 The command could not run — bad usage, or missing/unreadable input
2 Ran fine, but the result gates: NOT READY, a serious comparison regression, or insecure IaC

generate returns 0 even though its output is NOT READY by construction, because every generated
threat is deliberately left as Needs Investigation.

Verify your download

Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\ThreatModelReviewer-v2.1.0-x64.msi | Format-List Status, SignerCertificate
Get-FileHash .\ThreatModelReviewer-v2.1.0-x64.msi -Algorithm SHA256

Upgrading

Install over the top; settings, credentials and preferences are preserved. No model file format
changes, so existing .tm7 files and saved reports are unaffected.

name: Threat Model Reviewer v2.0.3
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer v2.0.3

Release date: 9 August 2026 · Platform: Windows 10/11 x64 · Type: Patch — documentation
and product copy. No functional change.

Threat Model Reviewer reviews, fixes and analyzes Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool (.tm7) threat
models — and OWASP Threat Dragon (.json) — catching the issues a Microsoft SDL reviewer would
send back before you submit. The readiness verdict and 0–100 score are deterministic and
computed entirely on your machine.

At a glance

Item Detail
What changed Product copy and documentation now describe exactly the capabilities that ship today
Who should update Everyone — this is the current supported release
Risk of updating Minimal: no engine, verdict, scoring or file-format changes
Downtime / migration None. Settings, credentials and preferences are preserved
Rollback Install any earlier 2.0.x package; configuration is forward/backward compatible

Changed

  • Product copy now matches the shipped feature set. The header subtitle, About dialog, package
    description and documentation previously described the app as also creating threat models.
    Model authoring is in beta and hidden in the desktop build, so every surface now reads
    "review, fix & analyze", and the Create capability — a guided wizard, plus Copilot drafting a
    data-flow diagram from a description, an architecture image or an OpenAPI spec — is clearly
    labelled beta.

    The create and openapi commands remain available in the CLI today for teams that want
    to author models programmatically.

  • Documentation raised to enterprise standard. New and expanded material for security review
    and managed rollout:

    • Data handling & privacy — every network destination, every on-disk path, the secret
      redaction applied before any AI prompt, and confirmation that the product collects no
      telemetry.
    • Enterprise deployment — silent install switches, MSI UpgradeCode and Inno AppId for
      detection rules, Intune / Configuration Manager / Group Policy guidance, how to disable update
      checks fleet-wide, air-gapped operation, and CI/CD gating with the CLI.
    • Third-party notices — full component inventory with licenses.
    • Security policy — vulnerability response targets, a supported-versions table, and the
      controls protecting the tool itself (untrusted-file parsing, prompt-injection detection,
      DPAPI credential storage, export formula-injection neutralization, supply chain).
    • Support policy — severity definitions and response targets.

Unchanged and guaranteed

  • The verdict and 0–100 review score remain 100% deterministic — produced by a fixed
    rubric engine with no AI dependency. Copilot is advisory only.
  • The full review works offline. No network access is required.
  • Your threat model never leaves your machine. AI features send only finding text and a
    redacted structural summary, never the .tm7 itself.

What ships in this release

Open a .tm7 or Threat Dragon .json and you get a stamped NOT READY / READY WITH NOTES
verdict, a 0–100 score with a letter grade, and a prioritized findings list — from roughly 70
deterministic checks spanning completeness and structure, STRIDE coverage, triage and mitigation
quality, security hygiene, and the AI/agentic surface (OWASP LLM Top 10 2025, OWASP Agentic,
MITRE ATLAS). Plus: an interactive diagram with write-back, a previewable remediation plan that
saves a corrected .tm7 which reopens cleanly in the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, deep
analysis (DREAD, attack trees, verification tests), and exports to HTML, PDF, Markdown, CSV,
JSON, SARIF and GitHub / Azure DevOps / Jira work items.

Updating

On v1.0.4 or later, the app updates itself: click Download & install on the in-app banner,
then Install & restart. Otherwise download a package below.

Administrators deploying centrally should follow
Enterprise deployment.

Downloads

Package Choose it when
…-x64.msi Standard installer; per-machine or per-user. Recommended, and the option for managed deployment
…-win-x64-portable.zip Extract and run — no installation
…-setup.exe Per-user installer, no administrator rights
…-x64.msix + …-publisher.cer MSIX (experimental — trust the .cer first; AI may be limited under MSIX)

Every build is self-contained — no .NET runtime installation required.
→ Install instructions

Verifying this release

Every artifact is Authenticode-signed. Before deploying widely:

Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\ThreatModelReviewer-v2.0.3-x64.msi | Format-List Status, SignerCertificate
Get-FileHash .\ThreatModelReviewer-v2.0.3-x64.msi -Algorithm SHA256

Artifacts are currently signed with a self-signed certificate (CN=ArasaniRohithReddy), so
Microsoft Defender SmartScreen may warn on first run — More info → Run anyway. Migration to a
CA/EV certificate or Azure Trusted Signing is planned and will require no change on the client.

Compatibility

Requirement Supported
Operating system Windows 10 (1809+) and Windows 11, x64
Runtime None required — self-contained
Input formats Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool .tm7; OWASP Threat Dragon .json
Optional AI GitHub Copilot (Individual / Business / Enterprise), or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint including Azure OpenAI

Support

  • Bugs and ideas — open an issue
  • Vulnerabilities — report privately, never in a public issue

Full history: CHANGELOG

name: Threat Model Reviewer v2.0.2
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer v2.0.2

An identity release: following the repository transfer, everything the app points at now uses the
canonical ArasaniRohithReddy home. No behavior changes — the verdict and score are untouched.

Changed

  • Canonical project home is now ArasaniRohithReddy. Every link and identifier the app carries has
    been updated to the new owner:

    • the in-app update check (so updates come from ArasaniRohithReddy/app-releases directly),
    • the About dialog and Help menu links — releases, install & user guide, FAQ, issues, security,
      and license,
    • the SARIF report's informationUri,
    • and the installer/package publisher, help/about URLs, and code-signing identity
      (CN=ArasaniRohithReddy).

    The old Rohithreddy7123 URLs still resolve through GitHub's automatic redirect, so existing installs
    are still offered this update     — after which they're fully canonical and no longer depend on the
    redirect.

Determinism

The verdict and 0–100 review score remain 100% deterministic and are never influenced by Copilot.

Updating

On v1.0.4 or later, the app updates in-app: click Download & install on the banner, then
Install & restart. Existing installs reach this release via GitHub's owner redirect.

MSIX note: because the package publisher changed, an existing MSIX install updates
side-by-side rather than in place. MSI, Setup.exe, and portable users update normally.

Downloads

Download Use it if…
…-x64.msi standard installer — choose all-users or just-me (recommended)
…-win-x64-portable.zip extract & run, no install
…-setup.exe per-user .exe installer (no admin)
…-x64.msix + …-publisher.cer MSIX (experimental — trust the .cer first; AI may be limited under MSIX)

→ Install instructions.
No .NET install needed (self-contained).

About the SmartScreen warning

The downloads are signed, but with a self-signed certificate for now, so Windows SmartScreen may still
warn on first run — More info → Run anyway. A CA/EV certificate or Azure Trusted Signing (planned)
removes the warning for everyone.

Found a bug or have an idea?
Open an issue.

name: Threat Model Reviewer v2.0.1
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer v2.0.1

A small follow-up to 2.0.0: a snappier diagram editor on large models, a friendlier CLI, and tighter
token handling.

Changed

  • Diagram edits no longer freeze the UI on large models. Adding, renaming, deleting, or connecting
    elements — and the Save changes and Reset commands on the Diagram tab — now run the re-parse and
    re-review on a background thread, so the app stays responsive even on big threat models.

Fixed

  • CLI: a dangling or unknown option (for example a trailing --model with no value) now prints a clear
    error and exits with code 1 instead of being silently treated as the input file; an unrecognized

name: Threat Model Reviewer v2.0.0
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer v2.0.0

A correctness release. Models you fix in the app now reliably reopen in the Microsoft Threat
Modeling Tool, Copilot's advisory text renders properly, and a whole-app audit (run with
Claude Opus 4.8 + Opus 5) hardened every write path.

Fixed

  • App-fixed .tm7 files now open in the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool. Two defects had
    made TMT reject a saved model as "could not be deserialized… or the threat model may be
    corrupted"    : the threat State was written in a human-readable form ("Needs Investigation")
    where TMT's enum requires the exact member name (NeedsInvestigation), and whole-model threats
    wrote empty GUID fields. Both are fixed and verified against TMT's own loader.
  • Fixed a TMT dashboard crash — "an item with the same key has already been added." TMT
    identifies a threat by TypeId + Source + Flow + Target, so several distinct threats added to a
    single element/category (for example multiple OWASP-LLM risks) now get distinct TypeIds and never
    collide.
  • The --baseline Create path no longer produces corrupt files (an XML declaration/encoding
    mismatch). The carried KnowledgeBase and multi-line names are preserved exactly.
  • Copilot output renders as formatted text. The whole-model critique, per-finding guidance, and
    mitigation plan now show real bold, italic, code, and bullet lists instead of literal
    ** and backticks.

Hardened (whole-app audit)

  • AI responses that are malformed, truncated, or fail entirely no longer crash the app or abort
    the deterministic report/verdict     — Copilot stays strictly advisory.
  • A triage-state parser no longer reads "not mitigated" / "needs mitigation" as Mitigated.
  • Model parsing, diff, and critique are robust to duplicate or blank element ids.
  • The portable-update helper can no longer hang invisibly; export CSVs are protected against
    spreadsheet formula-injection; the bundled Copilot runtime is never orphaned on exit.
  • Newly added diagram elements default in scope (a cloned template could previously flip them
    out-of-scope and change the deterministic result).

Determinism

The verdict and 0–100 review score remain 100% deterministic and are never influenced by
Copilot. Copilot only adds advisory guidance, critique, and drafted fixes that you choose to apply.

name: Threat Model Reviewer v1.0.9
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer v1.0.9

Fixes "Check for updates" wrongly reporting you're up to date.

What's fixed

  • The update check no longer misreports "You're on the latest version" when it actually failed.
    GitHub's unauthenticated API is limited to 60 requests/hour per network; when that limit was hit
    (HTTP 403), the app treated the failure as "up to date" — so a genuinely newer version wasn't
    offered.
    • It now falls back to the releases.atom feed (served from github.com and not subject to
      that API rate limit), so update checks keep working even when the API is throttled.
    • If GitHub really can't be reached, it now says "Couldn't reach GitHub… try again later"
      instead of claiming you're on the latest version.

If you were stuck on an older build that kept saying "you're on the latest," this release fixes it —
update once and future checks are reliable.

name: Threat Model Reviewer v1.0.0
body_html:
Threat Model Reviewer v1.0.0

First public release — a Windows desktop tool that reviews, fixes, analyzes, and
creates Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool (.tm7) threat models, powered by your own
GitHub Copilot seat. The verdict and 0–100 score are deterministic (never produced
by AI); Copilot is optional and advisory.

Downloads

Download Use it if…
...-win-x64-portable.zip You want the simplest option — extract and run. (recommended)
...-setup.exe You want a Start-Menu shortcut + uninstall entry (per-user, no admin).
...-x64.msix + ...-publisher.cer You prefer MSIX (experimental — AI features may be limited under MSIX sandboxing; trust the .cer first).

See install instructions.
No .NET install needed — every download is self-contained.

Highlights

  • Deterministic verdict + 0–100 review score with ~70 grounded rubric checks (structural,
    STRIDE coverage, triage/mitigation quality, identity/boundary, data protection, network,
    logging/detection, deprecated crypto, supply chain, mismodeled stencils, and a deep
    AI/agentic surface — OWASP LLM Top 10 2025, OWASP Agentic, MITRE ATLAS).
  • STRIDE coverage matrix, Threats-by-interaction, and a Framework coverage
    scorecard (OWASP Top 10 + STRIDE).
  • Fix with round-trip write-back to a valid .tm7; Create via a wizard or Copilot
    DFD extraction.
  • Optional Copilot enrichments (explain, deep analysis, draft fixes, critique, gap
    analysis, triage planning) — each independent and advisory.
  • Exports: HTML / PDF / Markdown / CSV / JSON / SARIF + work items (GitHub / Azure
    DevOps / Jira).

Notes

  • The portable .exe and installer aren't Authenticode-signed yet, so SmartScreen may warn
    on first run — More info → Run anyway.
  • Found a bug or have an idea? Open an issue.
